mcqs.question: In Spark's driver/executor architecture, what is the driver's role?
options: It stores all cached RDD data for the entire cluster
It is one of several interchangeable worker processes that run tasks
It runs the application's main logic, builds the execution plan, and coordinates tasks sent to executors, but does not run the bulk of the data processing itself
It replaces the cluster manager entirely once a job starts
mcqs.explanation: The driver plans and coordinates — breaking work into tasks and shipping them out — while executors are the ones that actually run tasks and hold cached data. Treating the driver as just another worker, or as the place cached data lives, or as replacing the cluster manager, all confuse the coordination role with the execution role.

mcqs.question: How does an RDD recover from losing a partition when an executor crashes, given that Spark doesn't replicate every partition the way HDFS replicates blocks?
options: It restores the partition from a hidden backup copy Spark keeps automatically
It requests a fresh copy of the partition from the cluster manager
It skips the lost partition and returns a partial, incomplete result
It recomputes the lost partition by replaying the recorded lineage of transformations that produced it
mcqs.explanation: Lineage is the mechanism — Spark remembers the sequence of transformations behind each partition and can replay just that sequence to rebuild what was lost, without needing a standing replica. There's no hidden backup or cluster-manager-supplied copy involved, and Spark doesn't silently return partial results for a lost partition — it recomputes to keep the result correct.

mcqs.question: Why does calling `.filter()` on a Spark DataFrame return instantly, even on a dataset with billions of rows?
options: Spark pre-loads a small sample of the data for every transformation call
Filter is a transformation — it only adds a step to the logical plan and doesn't touch any actual data until an action triggers execution
Filter only ever processes the first partition of the dataset
Spark caches every DataFrame automatically as soon as it's created
mcqs.explanation: Lazy evaluation means transformations like filter build a plan rather than execute anything, so the call returns immediately regardless of data size — the real work happens only when an action like collect or write is called. Spark doesn't sample data for transformation calls, doesn't limit itself to one partition, and does not cache DataFrames automatically; caching is an explicit, deliberate choice.

mcqs.question: What's the fundamental trade-off between Spark's lineage-based fault tolerance and HDFS's replication-based fault tolerance?
options: Lineage-based recovery pays a time cost only when a failure actually happens; replication pays a storage cost continuously, whether or not a failure ever occurs
Lineage-based recovery is strictly better in every scenario, which is why HDFS is considered obsolete
Replication-based recovery is only usable for streaming workloads, not batch
Lineage-based recovery requires three times the storage that replication requires
mcqs.explanation: The trade-off is genuinely two different costs paid on two different schedules — lineage recomputation costs time when a rare failure occurs, replication costs storage all the time as ongoing insurance. Neither approach is universally superior, HDFS replication isn't restricted to streaming use cases, and lineage-based recovery is specifically the technique that avoids paying replication's storage multiplier.

mcqs.question: A Spark job with 200 executors and plenty of aggregate cluster memory crashes with an out-of-memory error the moment `.collect()` is called on a billion-row DataFrame. Why does more executor memory not fix this?
options: Executors cannot hold more than one partition each, causing the crash
collect() always fails on datasets larger than 1 million rows regardless of memory
The cluster manager blocks any action that touches more than one executor
collect() pulls the entire result into the single driver process's memory, which is unrelated to the combined executor memory across the cluster
mcqs.explanation: The crash is specific to the driver, a single process that isn't sized like the executor fleet — collect() materializes the full result there, so cluster-wide executor memory is irrelevant to fixing it. There's no fixed row-count ceiling on collect(), no such cluster-manager restriction, and executors routinely hold many partitions each; none of those describe the actual failure.

mcqs.question: Why is reading Spark code by execution order (as if it ran line-by-line like ordinary sequential code) a common source of confusion for newcomers?
options: Because Spark code always executes in reverse of the order it's written
Because Spark requires all code to be written in a single line
Because transformations only build a logical plan, and the actual execution order and grouping is determined by the plan Spark builds when an action finally triggers it — not the line order
Because Python itself does not support sequential execution
mcqs.explanation: Lazy evaluation means the code's line order describes how the plan is built, not the order operations actually run — Spark can reorder, combine, or optimize steps across that plan before an action triggers real execution. Nothing about Spark reverses code order, single-line code isn't required, and this has nothing to do with Python's own execution model, which is perfectly sequential outside of Spark's lazy abstraction.
